title: An Hour Without a Price
placement: Proposed interlude after S1E06 and before the exclusive-supply offer in S1E07. Writer-only until adopted; never insert into the pilot.
text:
The wagon stood ready, which made the delay harder to explain.

Bale had checked the axle, the harness and the count. Eight sacks of ordinary grain waited beneath the canvas. No storm lay between the depot and the customer. The loading crew had finished early enough to eat before dark.

On the dispatch table, the permission box remained empty.

Corvin arrived with a new page.

"A small amendment," he said.

Bale looked at the page without touching it. "The order was paid yesterday."

"And yesterday we had not offered them a better arrangement."

"Does the better arrangement move the wagon?"

Corvin smiled as if Bale had accidentally made a joke. He set the amendment beside the receipt and weighted it with his narrow case.

Across the aisle, Veyra was speaking to a worker whose child had broken a wrist. She asked whether the splint could be kept dry on the way home. The worker nodded. She told him to leave at once and charged the missed hour to the depot.

Corvin waited until he had gone.

"That is why they trust you," he said.

"He needs to take his child home."

"Both things can be true."

Veyra looked at him. He lowered his eyes to the papers, choosing the expression of a person who had meant only a compliment.

The grain buyer was a small supplier outside the depot chain. Corvin’s amendment offered priority delivery in exchange for an exclusive season of purchases. He had written it elegantly. The old order would be released when the new agreement was accepted.

"You have put our signature on their hunger," Bale said.

"I have put a reliable schedule in front of an unreliable customer."

"They paid yesterday."

For a moment, only the loading crew could be heard. A buckle struck the wagon rail. Somewhere behind the east racks, a worker laughed at an ordinary mistake.

Veyra read the amendment twice. Then she moved Corvin’s case onto the bare tabletop.

"This order leaves under the terms it was bought."

"Of course. I was only—"

"You were changing the price after payment."

Bale reached for the dispatch pencil. Corvin put one finger on the new page.

"If every exception becomes public, we lose the value of the priority agreement."

"An existing agreement is not an exception."

He removed his finger.

Bale signed the release. The loading crew began moving before Corvin could explain how little he had intended. The wagon rolled down the clear aisle and out through the south doors. Eight sacks left the building. There would be eight fewer sacks to bargain with tomorrow.

Veyra watched until the sound of its wheels changed on the outer paving.

"Do not hold a paid order to manufacture a decision again," she said.

Corvin folded the rejected amendment carefully. "Understood."

Bale did not believe that the matter was finished. He believed that this wagon had left. Those were different-sized facts, and for once he was willing to keep them different.

Then Corvin opened his case a second time.

The paper he laid down was older. A charter account, copied from a record that had recently become inconveniently public. Veyra recognized the amount before she saw the date.

The second flood convoy.

At the bottom, the boat operator’s receipt recorded payment in full. Below it, in a smaller hand, someone had written that the rescued households owed no passage charge.

"They are speaking about it in the Burrow," Corvin said.

"They should have been speaking about it seven years ago."

"We could attach it to the new proposal. Remind them what dependable supply has already meant."

Veyra traced the edge of the copy without touching the writing. She remembered the original table: wet wood, a lamp that kept going out, a boat operator who would not promise a crossing until he had inspected the current himself. She had disliked the delay. Later she had understood why he insisted.

"The households owe no passage charge," Bale said.

Corvin gave him the tolerant look he reserved for people who insisted on reading the least useful sentence.

"I am not proposing a passage charge."

"Then leave that sentence visible."

Veyra looked up at Bale. He expected a reprimand for speaking twice. Instead she moved the copy away from the proposed contract.

"The rescue was paid for. Do not turn it into an unpaid bill."

Corvin paused. He had not expected to be corrected from both sides of the table.

"Would you prefer they think it meant nothing?"

The question landed. Veyra’s hand became still.

"It meant they came home."

She spoke quietly enough that the loading crew could not hear. Bale saw the answer cost her something, although not the thing Corvin had wanted it to cost.

For several breaths, the three stood beside a table holding a completed rescue and an unfinished bargain.

Then Veyra drew the new Burrow proposal toward her.

Its central term was unchanged: dependable supply in exchange for exclusive purchasing rights. She read the clause describing who could approve an alternative supplier. The answer was her office.

Bale waited.

Veyra corrected a number in the delivery estimate. She asked him to confirm the available wagons before the offer was carried to the Burrow. It was a sensible instruction. It made the promise more honest.

It did not make the condition acceptable.

Corvin gathered the papers that still had a future. This time he left the old rescue account on the table, its final sentence uncovered.

Outside, the grain wagon had already passed beyond the depot’s hearing. Veyra checked the empty permission box on another order and asked whose answer they were waiting for.

Bale told her the customer’s name.

She knew it. That, too, was part of the difficulty.
status: Complete prose; proposed chronology, not a dated episode commitment.

title: An Inventory of Names
placement: Proposed Ashmouth story after the failed season-one raid. It develops the later Dreg split; it is not a new event silently inserted into the season-one finale.
text:
Dreg had sorted the freight before he found the letter.

Food to the west cover. Dry rope to the east. A brass fitting too awkward to stack lay beside the share-count table, wrapped in cloth from the village it had been taken from.

The letter came back with a bag of meal he had sent to his cousin.

There were no accusations in it. That made it worse.

We can buy our own. Send theirs home.

He folded the paper along its old crease and put it beneath the short pencil in his vest.

Vessa landed beyond the east foot path, walked the final stretch and stopped beside the table. Dust had settled along the lower edges of her wings.

"Bad wind?" Dreg asked.

"Worse promises."

She studied the returned bag. "Family?"

He nodded.

She did not ask what the letter said. He was grateful until he realized she probably knew.

The brass fitting belonged to a village pump. Dreg knew the village because he had written it in his private book. He had written the date, the original cargo mark, the place it was taken and the share he had received. If Brakka ever accused him of stealing from the band, the book could prove exactly how much he was owed.

It could prove other things as well. He had tried not to think about those as the purpose of a useful record.

Brakka arrived while he was measuring a replacement strap.

Two people followed her carrying a torn piece of convoy canvas. She ordered them to stretch it across the loading platform where it would be visible from the west approach. She wanted the next travelers to recognize whose cloth it was.

"And the spoiled freight goes under it," she said.

Dreg looked at the sacks. "None of that is spoiled."

"Then it will make a clear message."

He understood before she said the rest. A display at the platform. Burned supplies beneath a captured mark. Something dramatic enough to make a failed raid sound like the beginning of a greater one.

He kept both hands on the strap.

"We need those."

"We need them frightened."

"Frightened sacks do not feed anyone."

One of the carriers looked down. The other pretended to be occupied with a knot.

Brakka stepped closer to the table. Her shadow crossed the returned bag.

"You have become very interested in what cannot be done."

Dreg could have explained the count. He could have shown the meals remaining, the damaged harnesses and the cost of replacing the rope. He had made those arguments before. Sometimes Brakka listened because the numbers gave her a way to call restraint her own decision.

This time she wanted witnesses.

"I will not move food there to be burned," he said.

Vessa went still. The wind pulled once at her coral map ribbon.

Brakka’s first response was disbelief, carefully disguised as patience. She told Dreg that the freight belonged to the crew. He had no right to decide what happened to it.

He thought of the book beneath his bedroll. How often had he used that same sentence, changing only the name of the owner?

"It belonged to someone before us."

"Now you remember?"

The contempt was deserved in a way she had not intended.

"Yes," he said. "Now."

Nobody on the platform moved.

Brakka turned to the two carriers and repeated the order. One took a step toward the food stacks. The other asked which sacks were already marked for supper.

The question was small, practical and disastrous for the performance. It required someone to admit that the destroyed food would have to be replaced by something they did not have.

Dreg took the pump fitting from beside the table and set it on a handcart. He added the returned meal bag. Then he went to the refuge lodge.

Vessa followed as far as the door.

"If you leave with goods, she will call it theft."

"She may be right about the wrong part."

He took out the book.

Vessa glanced at the open page. Her own route payment appeared beside a village name.

"That is not only yours."

"I know."

For the first time, she looked afraid of him. Not because he could overpower her. Because an ordinary, accurate entry could reach someone she could no longer avoid by taking to the air.

"You could remove that line."

He held the page flat with one hand.

"Then I would still be keeping it for myself."

Outside, Brakka had begun telling the carriers what his departure would mean. No share. No protection. No welcome if he returned asking for work. She made it sound like the removal of gifts rather than the end of a bargain.

Dreg wrapped the book in the pump cloth. He left his share tokens on the empty bedroll. The tokens had once been the most reassuring objects he owned.

At the west approach, Brakka stood beside the handcart.

"You expect them to thank you?"

He looked at the bag his cousin had returned.

"No."

"They will ask where the rest is."

"I wrote that down."

For a moment, he thought she would overturn the cart. Instead she stepped aside and let him take it where the others could see. She had already decided how to describe the scene: a weak worker, a stolen share, a captain too strong to be troubled by either.

Vessa watched from the yard. She did not accompany him. She had not warned every convoy, and his book would not let her pretend she had.

Dreg took the broad wagon approach slowly. The fitting made the cart pull to one side. At the first level patch, he stopped and adjusted its weight instead of forcing the wheel.

He could not carry back everything that had been taken. He could carry the record of it, and stop calling the limit a reason to return nothing.

Behind him, the yard still held people who might obey Brakka’s next order. Ahead, people were entitled to ask questions he did not want to answer.

He checked the strap again, made certain the book was dry, and continued.
status: Complete prose; proposed chronology, not a dated episode commitment.
